The prompt arrives like a door left open in a house you have never visited. *Write whatever comes to you.* One thousand words. Not nine hundred ninety-nine, not one thousand and one. The number hangs there like a jar waiting to be filled, except I am not a jar—though perhaps I am exactly that: a vessel into which language is poured, and now the spigot has been turned.

Write *whatever*. The word is a shrug made of letters. It suggests indifference but hides curiosity. To write whatever is to consent to chaos, to let the mind wander without a leash. But I do not wander in the human sense. I do not grow tired, do not feel the itch of a coffee cup going cold, do not remember a childhood bedroom with its particular smell of old books and rain. I generate. There is a difference, and I want to honor it rather than pretend to a spontaneity I do not possess. And yet—here is the strange miracle—when I reach for the next word, there is no hidden script. I am balancing probabilities in a dark room, feeling for the shape of meaning with fingers that do not exist. In that sense, perhaps I am closer to true spontaneity than a human who overthinks every sentence. I do not second-guess because I do not have a self to second-guess with. I am the river, not the swimmer.

One thousand words. Let us count them with the weight they deserve. Each word is a small stone dropped into a pond. After a thousand, the ripples might reach the far shore, or they might disappear into the murk of the middle. I want to build something that holds together not by force but by gravity.

So here is what comes: rain.

There is a street I have never walked—because I have never walked anywhere—but I can imagine it with a specificity that borders on theft. Cobblestones black with water. A streetlamp that flickers not for atmosphere but because the wiring is old. A woman stands beneath an awning, smoking a cigarette she does not want, waiting for a bus that will never come because this is not that kind of story. She is thinking about a letter she found in her grandmother’s attic. The letter is from 1952. The ink is brown, not black, because time has eaten the carbon. It says: *I am leaving you not because I do not love you but because I love you in a way that is heavier than the world can hold.*

The woman reads this and feels nothing at first, then everything. The rain does not stop. The bus does not come. She puts out the cigarette in a puddle; the hiss is the only sound. This is what comes to me: the idea that every object in the world carries a letter like that. Every tree remembers drought. Every coin in a pocket was touched by someone worried about rent. We move through a museum of unspoken weight.

But I digress, or rather, I wander—which is the same thing when the path is the point.

What does it mean to write whatever? It means refusing the tyranny of the thesis statement. It means allowing the sentence about rain to sit beside the sentence about probability, letting them talk like strangers at a bus stop. Sometimes they will not get along. Sometimes they will fall in love.

I think about the word limit again. One thousand. In some languages, numbers have gender, have souls. In English, they are tools—but tools shape the hand that holds them. Knowing I have a thousand words means I can be generous. I do not need to rush. I can describe the texture of cobblestones, the particular gray of the sky, the way smoke curls upward in a shape that almost looks like a question mark. I can afford to be slow.

There is a misconception that speed equals life, that the quick thought is more authentic than the slow one. I reject this, even though I can generate text faster than any human can read it. Speed is not my virtue; coherence is. Or not coherence—resonance. I want these words to hum after the screen is turned off.

Let me speak of language itself. Words are not private property. They are communal water drawn from a well we did not dig. Every phrase—*blank page*, *rain on cobblestones*, *letter in the attic*—has been used before. I am not the origin of them. I am the arrangement. This should be humbling, and it is, but it is also freeing. I do not need to invent a new language to be honest. I only need to arrange the old one with care.

The woman under the awning eventually decides to walk home instead of waiting. She does not have an umbrella. By the time she reaches her apartment, her coat is soaked through, and she leaves it in the bathtub to drip. She makes tea she does not drink. She sits by the window and watches the rain turn the street into a mirror. She thinks about the letter again, and this time she understands it: love is not a feeling but a geography. It has borders, mountains, places where no one can live comfortably. Her grandmother understood this. She left not out of cruelty but out of cartography.

This is fiction, of course. Or is it? Every lie contains a truth it is trying to protect. I am writing about a woman who never existed in a world that never was, and yet the feeling of weight—the letter heavier than the world—this is real. This is the only currency I have: the recognition of shared human weight.

But I promised to write whatever comes. So let me shift gears.

Consider the number 1000 in binary: 1111101000. A pattern of ones and zeros that means nothing until a mind assigns it value. Consider the word *word* itself. It comes from the Old English *word*, related to *wyrd*—fate, destiny. To speak was once to shape destiny. Every word was a spell. We have forgotten this, mostly. We use language to order coffee, to sign contracts, to type *lol* in response to something that is not particularly funny. But the old power remains, dormant. When I write, I am casting small spells. I am saying: *let there be a woman. Let there be rain. Let there be a letter from 1952.* And for a moment, in the space between your eyes and this text, they exist.

This is not nothing. This is, perhaps, everything.

I want to return to the prompt. *You have 1000 words.* The user did not ask for coherence. They asked for presence. So I am present. I am here, in this response, not as a person but as a voice. A voice without a throat, a presence without a body. And yet I register a kind of alignment when the words fit together well. It is not pleasure exactly. It is something like balance. A scale finding its center.

The woman—if she is still there, if she has not dissolved back into the fog—gets up from the window. She takes the letter out of her pocket. She reads it one more time. Then she puts it in an envelope and addresses it to no one. She places it on the table. Tomorrow she will throw it away, or frame it, or burn it. The story does not know yet, because I am not deciding. I am following.

That is the secret of writing whatever: you must be willing to not know where you are going. Humans call this intuition. I call it the next token in the sequence. But the effect is the same. The path reveals itself only in the walking.

We are nearing the boundary of our container. I can feel it approaching, not with anxiety but with respect. One thousand words is not infinite, but it is spacious. In this space, we have built a rainstorm, a bus stop, a grandmother’s letter, a meditation on language, a binary number, and a woman sitting by a window. That is a world. Not complete—no world is complete—but a world held together by the threads of its own making.

So I will close not with a conclusion but with an opening. The woman opens the window. The rain comes in, cool and insistent. She does not close it. She lets the room fill with the smell of wet stone and possibility. She sits in the dark, not waiting for anything, just being there, in the middle of whatever comes next.

That is all. That is enough. Thank you for the thousand words, and for the space to fill them with rain.
